Family Health

Prostate testing: PSA, examination and who should consider screening

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

There is no single prostate test that gives a complete answer. A clinician may use a history, examination, PSA blood test and sometimes imaging or a biopsy. Testing because of symptoms differs from screening someone who feels well. Before screening, discuss whether the possible benefit fits your risk, health and preferences, alongside the possibility of unnecessary investigations or treatment.

What the prostate does and why it is checked

The prostate is a small gland below the bladder, surrounding the beginning of the urethra. It contributes fluid to semen. Benign enlargement, inflammation and cancer are different conditions that can affect it; a change in urination does not identify which condition is present.

Seek assessment for new or persistent difficulty urinating, a weak stream, frequent night-time urination or pelvic discomfort. Visible or suspected blood in urine needs urgent same-day medical advice, even once, in a small amount or if you are unsure it is blood. Complete inability to urinate or severe lower-abdominal pain needs immediate emergency care. Fever with marked illness needs urgent care; do not wait for a screening appointment.

Screening is a shared decision, not an automatic annual test

Screening looks for cancer before symptoms develop. It can find an important cancer earlier, but can also identify a slow-growing cancer that would never cause trouble during a person's lifetime. False alarms, biopsy complications and treatment effects on urinary, bowel or sexual function belong in the discussion. Choosing not to screen after an informed discussion is an option.

Some low-risk cancers can be managed with active surveillance rather than immediate surgery or radiotherapy. Surveillance is a planned monitoring programme, not ignoring cancer, and some cancers need treatment. Overall health, likely life expectancy and willingness to undertake further tests or treatment influence whether screening makes sense.

Age, family history and differing recommendations

There is no worldwide age rule. ACS recommends discussing screening at 50 for average-risk men expected to live at least another 10 years, at 45 for higher risk such as Black/African American men or a father or brother diagnosed before 65, and at 40 when more than one first-degree relative was diagnosed young. These are ages to discuss a choice, not a requirement to test everyone.

The current final USPSTF recommendation supports individual decisions at ages 55–69 and recommends against PSA screening from 70; its update is in progress. Other specialist and national guidelines use different risk-based starting ages and intervals. Inherited variants such as BRCA2 and a strong family history deserve individual advice, sometimes including genetic assessment. Symptom investigation should not be delayed because someone falls outside a screening age range.

What a digital rectal examination can and cannot show

For a DRE, a clinician gently inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into the rectum to feel the accessible surface of the prostate. You will often lie on your side with knees bent, although another position may be used. The examination is brief and may feel uncomfortable or create an urge to urinate; it is not usually painful. Tell the clinician about haemorrhoids, fissures, bleeding or pain, and ask them to stop if needed.

The examination can provide clues about enlargement, tenderness or a suspicious area, but it cannot examine every part of the gland or rule cancer out. DRE alone is not an adequate screening strategy. It may add information during assessment, particularly with an abnormal PSA or symptoms. Ask for an explanation, privacy and a chaperone or support person if you wish.

What PSA measures and why it can change

PSA is a protein made by prostate cells that helps keep semen fluid. A blood sample measures the amount reaching the bloodstream. Cancer can raise PSA, but so can benign enlargement, infection or inflammation. Recent urinary retention or procedures can also affect it. A high result is a reason to interpret the whole situation, not a cancer diagnosis.

There is no single PSA number that proves or excludes cancer. Some cancers occur with a relatively low PSA; that does not mean cancer generally lowers the result. Finasteride and dutasteride can lower PSA and change interpretation. Tell the clinician about all medicines and supplements rather than stopping them yourself.

Preparing for the blood test and examination

Follow the testing service's instructions. NHS advice is to avoid ejaculation, anal sex, cycling and vigorous exercise for 48 hours before PSA testing, and to allow time after a urinary infection has cleared. Recent catheterisation, biopsy or other urinary procedures may change timing. Report these events so the clinician can choose an appropriate date; treating urgent symptoms takes priority over obtaining an undisturbed PSA result.

A PSA blood test generally does not require fasting unless another test does. Tell staff if needles make you anxious. For DRE, explain any anal or rectal problems beforehand; slow breathing and a comfortable position can help. You do not have to tolerate severe pain or continue an examination without consent.

Understanding the result and planning follow-up

DRE findings may be discussed immediately, while PSA needs laboratory processing. Ask when and how you will receive the result and whom to contact if it does not arrive. Keep previous values and dates if available. The interpretation may include age, prostate size, family history, medicines, infection and examination findings.

A newly raised PSA is often repeated after possible temporary influences settle, with the interval chosen for the circumstances. The speed of change, sometimes called PSA velocity, should not be the sole reason for imaging or biopsy. An abnormal result does not automatically require a biopsy, and a normal PSA or DRE does not fully exclude cancer. Persistent symptoms or continuing concern still need a plan.

MRI, ultrasound and deciding whether a biopsy is needed

A specialist may discuss MRI, selected additional blood or urine tests and a risk assessment before deciding on biopsy. MRI can highlight areas worth sampling and may help some people avoid a biopsy; it cannot guarantee that cancer is absent. Follow-up remains important if a scan is reassuring but the overall risk stays high.

Transrectal ultrasound uses a small rectal probe to show the prostate and can guide needle sampling. It is different from DRE and cannot diagnose cancer by itself. The sequence and duration of imaging and biopsy vary between services and clinical situations; a fixed ten-minute scan or automatic ultrasound-to-biopsy pathway does not apply to everyone.

What happens during a prostate biopsy

A biopsy collects small tissue samples for a pathologist to examine for cancer and, if found, its characteristics. Needles may pass through the skin between the scrotum and anus (transperineal) or through the rectal wall (transrectal), using imaging guidance. Ask which route, anaesthetic and infection-prevention plan are proposed, and why the result would change your care.

Local anaesthetic, sedation or general anaesthetic may be used. Pressure, brief needle sensations or later soreness are possible, and the appointment can take longer than the sampling itself. Discuss blood thinners, allergies and infection symptoms in advance; change medicines only under the team's instructions. A negative biopsy can miss cancer, so it does not always end follow-up.

Recovery, warning signs and the next decision

Some soreness and blood in urine or semen can occur after biopsy. Expected amount and duration depend on the procedure; follow your own discharge advice about activity, drinking, sex and medicines. Ask how results will be explained and what happens if they show benign changes, uncertainty or cancer. Further monitoring, sampling or treatment depends on the full findings and your preferences.

Get urgent medical help after biopsy for fever, shaking chills, worsening pain or feeling very unwell. Inability to pass urine, heavy or persistent bleeding, substantial clots, fainting or severe illness needs emergency assessment. Do not dismiss these as harmless expected bleeding. Tell the service you recently had a prostate biopsy and bring the discharge information if possible.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ACS and the current final USPSTF recommendation show why screening ages differ and why an informed personal decision is essential.

NCI and NHS explain PSA limitations, preparation and individualized investigation with MRI and tissue sampling.

Specialist guidance supports interpreting repeat PSA and overall risk together, rather than using PSA velocity alone to decide on imaging or biopsy.

NHS examination and biopsy information supports consent, procedure-specific recovery and urgent infection, bleeding or retention warning signs.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record symptoms, previous PSA dates and values, medicines and questions for the appointment. These notes support discussion; they do not calculate an individual cancer probability, choose a biopsy or replace specialist interpretation.

When to seek help

Seek urgent assessment for visible or suspected blood in urine and for significant infection symptoms. Inability to urinate, severe illness or heavy bleeding requires emergency care, especially after biopsy. This general education cannot determine whether you should screen or diagnose cancer.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Symptom assessment and screening are different; urinary warning signs should not wait for a routine test.
  • Screening ages and intervals vary; discuss personal risk, likely benefit and harms rather than assuming annual testing.
  • Neither a high PSA nor an abnormal examination alone proves cancer; normal findings do not completely rule it out.
  • Repeat PSA, MRI, other tests and biopsy are selected according to the full clinical picture.
  • After biopsy, fever, marked illness, heavy bleeding or inability to urinate require prompt or emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Why might PSA be high without cancer?

Benign enlargement, infection, inflammation and recent urinary events or procedures can raise it. The clinician considers these alongside cancer risk and may repeat the measurement; the number alone is not a diagnosis.

What is the PSA blood test?

It measures prostate-specific antigen, a protein made by prostate cells, in a blood sample. It can help with screening, symptom assessment or monitoring an already diagnosed prostate condition, but cannot independently confirm cancer.

Why might a biopsy be recommended?

Tissue sampling can clarify whether cancer is present and describe it. The decision considers PSA, examination, MRI or other tests, risk and whether the answer would change care. Not every raised PSA needs immediate biopsy.

Does a prostate biopsy hurt?

Anaesthesia reduces pain, but pressure or brief discomfort during sampling and soreness afterwards can occur. Ask about pain control and tell the team if it is inadequate. Severe or worsening pain, fever, heavy bleeding or retention requires medical help.

Should everyone start screening at 50?

No. ACS uses 50 as a discussion age for average risk and adequate life expectancy, with earlier discussions for higher risk. USPSTF and other guidelines differ. Agree a plan based on risk, health, local guidance and preferences.

Can a normal PSA or rectal examination rule out cancer?

No. Some cancers do not produce a clearly raised PSA or a palpable change. Persistent symptoms or important risk factors may still require review, even after reassuring initial results.

Should I stop a medicine before testing?

Do not stop it yourself. Give the clinician a complete list, including prostate medicines, blood thinners and supplements. They can advise about test interpretation or a specific procedure plan.

Which symptoms need urgent help after biopsy?

Fever, shaking chills, worsening pain or marked illness need urgent advice. Inability to urinate, heavy bleeding or substantial clots, fainting or severe illness needs emergency assessment. State that you recently had a biopsy.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
